questions.script: Our class is visiting the nature reserve tomorrow, so I checked the forecast again. Yesterday it showed sunshine, and this morning someone mentioned strong winds. sections.script:
Interviewer: Today we are speaking to Hind, a young weather scientist, about staying safe during floods. Why do wadis sometimes become dangerous?
Hind: Heavy rain can fill a dry wadi very quickly. The water may look shallow, but it can be strong enough to move a car.
Interviewer: What should families do when an alert arrives?
Hind: They should check official information, keep away from flooded roads and move to a safe place if advised. Nobody should try to cross flowing water.
Interviewer: How can students prepare?
Hind: At our school, pupils helped make an emergency plan. We practised moving calmly to the upper floor and learned where the first-aid supplies were stored.
Interviewer: Is safety only the responsibility of adults?
Hind: No. Young people can remind others to avoid danger, save water at home and take weather warnings seriously. Even small actions matter.
Interviewer: What did you learn from the last exercise?
Hind: The most useful lesson was to prepare before a storm, not while the water is rising. Clear instructions helped everyone feel confident.

After a storm damaged part of the beach near her village, Mariam joined a student team that wanted to protect the coast. At first, the volunteers thought the problem was simply the plastic bottles left by visitors. However, a marine researcher showed them small pieces of fishing line hidden between the rocks. These could be even more dangerous because birds and turtles might become trapped in them.

The team divided the beach into four sections. Each group recorded the types of rubbish it found, using gloves and reusable collection bags. Mariam's group counted thirty-six plastic items on the first morning, but the researcher reminded them that a single day's figures could be misleading. They returned twice more before drawing conclusions.

The pupils then interviewed visitors. Most people said they wanted a cleaner beach, but many could not find a rubbish bin nearby. Instead of blaming visitors, the students suggested adding labelled recycling points at the entrance. The local council agreed to try the idea for one month.

Four weeks later, the number of plastic items had fallen noticeably. Mariam was pleased, although she understood that one improvement would not solve every environmental problem. She presented the results at school and asked younger pupils to continue collecting data. The project taught her that protecting nature needs careful observation, cooperation and long-term effort.

questions.script: Our activity leader offered three choices for Saturday. We could sail near the harbour, walk through the forest, or follow the cycling track across the hills. Most pupils had already tried sailing and walking, so we finally voted for mountain biking.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Adventure Hour. Faris, tell us about your first overnight camping trip.
Faris: We went to a mountain campsite with two trained instructors. I had packed everything the night before, but I still forgot my torch.
Interviewer: Did that cause a problem?
Faris: Not really. My friend had brought a spare one, and we checked the equipment together before setting off. The instructors reminded us never to walk away from the group by ourselves.
Interviewer: What was the most difficult activity?
Faris: We crossed a narrow path in the afternoon. The wind became stronger, so the leader told us to move slowly and keep a safe distance from the edge.
Interviewer: Did the bad weather spoil the whole trip?
Faris: No. We changed our plans, returned to the campsite and cooked dinner together. The next morning, the weather was calmer, and we watched the sunrise.
Interviewer: Would you go again?
Faris: Definitely. I learned that being prepared is more important than being brave. You should always listen to experienced guides and check the forecast before you travel.

When Hamad joined a weekend mountain-biking trip, he was certain that cycling quickly would impress his friends. He had ridden on flat roads many times, but he had never explored a rocky mountain track. His instructor, Aisha, explained that controlling a bicycle safely mattered more than finishing first.

Before they left the camp, everyone checked their helmets and brakes. Hamad realised that he had forgotten to fill his water bottle, so he returned to the tent while the others waited. He felt embarrassed, but Aisha told him that checking equipment carefully was a sign of responsibility.

The group followed a path through a narrow valley. After they had climbed the first hill, the wind began to rise. Hamad tried to overtake another rider, but his front wheel slipped on loose stones. He stopped himself before falling and waited until the path was clear. Aisha helped him choose a safer speed.

At midday, the cyclists reached a shaded rest area. They shared snacks and watched the sunlight moving across the mountains. Hamad noticed that the quieter pupils had seen birds, interesting rocks and an old trail marker that he had missed while rushing.

When the group returned, Hamad wrote about the trip in his journal. He decided to practise his balance and learn more about mountain safety before attempting a harder route. The greatest discovery had not been his speed, but the confidence that came from making thoughtful decisions.

sections.script:
Interviewer: Welcome to Money Matters. Dana, your class recently tried a saving challenge. How did it work?
Dana: Each pupil chose a personal goal and recorded spending for four weeks. I wanted to save for a second-hand bicycle, while my friend hoped to buy a tablet.
Interviewer: Was saving easy at first?
Dana: No. I often bought snacks without checking how much I had left. Our teacher suggested writing down every purchase before deciding whether it was necessary.
Interviewer: Did the class learn anything about shopping?
Dana: We compared prices at several shops and learned to keep receipts. One student exchanged a damaged item rather than throwing it away. We also discovered that buying something on sale does not always mean saving money.
Interviewer: What happened at the end?
Dana: I had saved enough for the bicycle, but I decided to wait until I could check its condition carefully. Some students donated part of their savings to a local charity.
Interviewer: What advice would you give younger pupils?
Dana: Choose a realistic goal, compare prices and think before you buy. A little patience can make your money go much further.

For several months, Reem had wanted to buy a camera. She enjoyed taking photographs with her phone, but her cousin owned a camera that could produce clearer pictures. Reem saved some of her weekly pocket money and searched online for a suitable model. At first, she was attracted by an expensive advertisement offering several extra accessories.

Her older brother suggested comparing prices before making a decision. They visited two shops and discovered that the same camera cost considerably less in the second one. Reem almost bought it immediately, but then she remembered that she had planned to help pay for a school trip as well.

A week later, a neighbour offered to sell Reem a used camera. The price was reasonable, and the neighbour allowed her to test it in daylight and indoors. One button was loose, so Reem asked how much a repair would cost. The shop assistant explained that the camera could be repaired cheaply, but she advised Reem to keep the receipt for any new parts.

Reem discussed the choices with her family. She decided not to buy the camera that week. Instead, she borrowed her cousin's camera for the school photography exhibition and continued saving. By the end of term, she had enough money for both the school trip and a reliable camera. She realised that waiting and asking questions had helped her make a better decision.
